title: 10M byte-level language model on real text: Rouge-LM vs a 10M Transformer
follows: R1.03 (small state + memory), R1.09 (cheap reads), R1.11 (local window + state: PASS), R1.12 (streaming: PASS, seed-unstable; LSTM retains perfectly), R1.13 (hand-made forgetting: FAIL)
question: At 10M parameters and the same training bytes of real text (enwik8), does Rouge-LM (local window + a few gated state slots per layer, constant inference memory) (a) match a standard Transformer at equal visible context, and (b) use context beyond the Transformer's window through its state, at a fraction of the inference memory?

design.rouge-lm: block-recurrent: blocks of 64 bytes; each byte attends to 16 state slots of its layer, the previous block and its own block causally; after each block the slots read the block through the bytes' keys/values and update with a learned forget gate (bias +2, keep). The R1.12/R1.13 lesson (a learned gate retains, a hand-made allocation rule does not) is built in; the R1.09 lesson (a cheap read) is the shared keys/values. Trained with its state carried across consecutive segments of each stream (truncated backpropagation through time).
design.window: the same code with 0 slots: a sliding-window Transformer (window 64-127 bytes). The ablation that isolates the state.
design.transformer: GPT-style decoder with full causal attention over its 256-byte training segment; no state, no cache between segments.
design.lstm: 2-layer LSTM, the classic recurrent baseline, state carried like rouge-lm.
design.same_data: all models read the same byte streams in the same order (16 streams, 256 bytes per step)

setup.hardware: GitHub-hosted CPU runners (tier 0, $0), up to 2 resumable attempts per run

compute.cpu_flops_measured: 3 x 19.8 MFLOP/byte (torch FLOP counter, Transformer) x 2822 bytes/s = 168 GFLOP/s on a 4-core container (2026-09-30); 8e10 assumes a GitHub runner at half that

predictions.PASS: rouge-lm is within 0.03 BPB of the Transformer at equal visible context (L1), at least 0.02 BPB better on bytes 1k-4k of long test streams (L3), with at most half its inference memory (L4, analytic: 1.2 MiB vs 5.0 MiB). A PASS is the advantage that R1.15 (50M) requires.
predictions.PARTIAL: any of L1, L2 (state beats the same model without state on 1k-4k by 0.02) or L3.
predictions.priors: the Transformer (full attention over 256 bytes) is expected to be best on valid.bpb; rouge-lm sees only 64-127 bytes exactly plus 16 slots per layer, so L1 is uncertain; L2 is the cleanest test of the state; the LSTM (L5, reported) is a strong small-scale byte model.
predictions.flops: rouge-lm executes 15.8 MFLOP/byte vs 19.8 for the Transformer (20% fewer) at 2.6% more parameters; this is reported, not gated.
predictions.undertraining: 8000 steps x 4096 bytes = 32.8M training bytes (0.36 epochs) is far below compute-optimal for 10M parameters; absolute BPB will be high (expected 1.6-2.2) and only the comparison at equal bytes is claimed.

prior_art: Block-Recurrent Transformer 2203.07852, Recurrent Memory Transformer 2207.06881, Transformer-XL 1901.02860, Griffin 2402.19427, Longformer local attention 2004.05150, enwik8 byte-level LM (Hutter prize; Al-Rfou et al. 1808.04444)
not_claimed: Segment recurrence and local attention are prior art. The question is only whether Rouge's slot state earns its place against a Transformer at equal parameters and bytes, on real text, at tier-0 scale.
